newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks may slip further but losses capped.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks may slip further but losses capped.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market could slip further if overseas investors sell their Japanese shares for short-term profits, but any losses would not be very large, brokers and analysts said on Friday.
Wall Street's tumble knocked the wind out of the Tokyo stock market's sails on Friday, sending the Nikkei index below the key 20,000 point line for the first time in more than three months.
The 225-issue Nikkei average fell by more than 500 points during the session before recovering somewhat by the close. It ended down 159.81 points, or 0.78 percent, at 20,341.39.

"We are not very pessimistic about the outlook, although much depends on New York tonight," said Hideo Sakaguchi, general manager of the securities investment department at the Meiji Life Insurance Company.

He cited Japanese economic fundamentals as the reason behind the optimism, with the economy still in the process of gradual recovery. "Today's loss was not like a free-fall, driven by panic sales." He said that investor demand would support the Nikkei average at below the 20,000 line.
On Thursday in New York, the Dow industrials shed nearly 100 points in the biggest point loss since mid-July.
The Dow dropped like a stone in the last hour of trade, losing 1.54 percent to close at about 6,304.
Brokers said that the next chart point for the Nikkei 225 average was 19,920.02, a low marked on September 3.
Kiyoshi Kimura, general manager of the research department at Societe Generale Securities Ltd, said that the index could dip below 20,000 again, but major technical support would be found at 18,500.
Shinichi Ichikawa, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities, said the Nikkei average would remain underpinned by demand from domestic pension funds until the end of the year.

"For the rest of the year, buying from investors such as public pension funds will support the market," Shinichi Ichikawa, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities, told Reuters Financial Television.

But he said the market could be vulnerable in the first three months next year, partly because of expected selling from domestic institutional investors towards the end of this business year in March 1997.
Brokers said the downturn on Wall Street dampened market hopes in Tokyo that foreign investors would carry on their selective buying of Japanese blue-chips.
The Nikkei average's recent rally was led by foreign investors' active buying of shares in blue-chip companies which showed strong growth in profits and rosy outlooks.
Global stock markets have been nervous since Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan talked about the possibility of equity markets rising too fast.
The head of the U.S. central bank said last week that "irrational exuberance" could be affecting the markets.
Since then, sell-offs on the Big Board have depressed the Tokyo market.
